Lecture 1: Declarative Components versus Manual DOM

Interview Question

CORE

What is React, and how does its declarative, component-based model differ from plain JavaScript DOM scripting?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. A subscriber named Elena updates her account name on The National Times website.
  2. The webpage displays her name in ten separate places across the screen.
  3. Elena saves her new name, but your code updates nine spots and misses the tenth.
  4. Why does that tenth tag on the screen still show her old name?
  5. Conflicting names confuse the subscriber and make the website look broken and unreliable.
  6. The computer holds the new name in memory, but the webpage cannot update itself.
  7. Today you learn how React replaces manual updates and keeps your whole interface in sync.

The Fragility of Manual DOM Scripting

On any content website like The National Times, reader data appears across many independent sections at once. When a subscriber logs into the site, their name appears in the top navigation greeting, in the subscriber status profile, in the comment box, and in the account drawer. In traditional JavaScript development, keeping all ten locations accurate requires you to write manual browser commands for each spot. When the reader renames their account, your script must locate every single HTML element on the page and rewrite its text content by hand.

To understand why this approach fails at scale, consider what that manual script actually looks like in practice. You write selectors such as document.getElementById('greeting-text') and document.querySelector('.header-user') You assign the new name directly to the textContent property of each element. If your page has ten places showing that name, you write ten separate queries and ten separate property assignments.

DO NOT DO THIS: Never write manual DOM queries, defensive null checks, and imperative property mutations across application scripts.

Manual DOM Script
1function updateReaderName(newName) {
2 const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting-text');
3 if (greeting) greeting.textContent = `Welcome back, ${newName}`;
WRONG: manually queries and mutates each NODE
4 const subscriber = document.getElementById('subscriber-user');
5 if (subscriber) subscriber.textContent = `Subscriber: ${newName}`;
WRONG: breaks silently if an ID changes
6}

Notice how fragile this pattern is in practice. The script relies entirely on hardcoded string identifiers like 'greeting-text' and 'subscriber-user'. If an HTML designer renames an element ID or moves the subscriber profile into a breaking news header, document.getElementById fails silently and returns null. Because of the defensive if (subscriber) guard clause, the browser does not throw a loud error: it simply skips the mutation. The tenth element is never updated, and no warning appears in the developer console to alert you.

This quiet failure triggers state drift (the divergence where computer memory holds the updated data, but the live webpage still renders stale text). The JavaScript variable holds the reader's new name, but the browser DOM remains frozen in the past. To prevent this drift, the programmer is forced to act as a human bookkeeping engine, manually memorizing every DOM node that displays the name and ensuring no update command is ever omitted.

This failure reveals the core problem of imperative DOM scripting (the programming style where you write explicit, step-by-step commands instructing the browser exactly how to find and mutate each individual document node). Imperative code acts like a passenger giving turn-by-turn driving directions: turn left, drive two hundred meters, turn right, and stop. If the passenger forgets one turn, the car ends up in the wrong neighborhood. In web applications, if your imperative script misses one DOM node, the screen shows incorrect data.

⚡ IN THE WILD

What does imperative vs declarative really mean? Imagine a subscriber named Elena logs into The National Times. Her name appears in ten different places across the screen, from the sidebar to the navigation bar. But what happens when she updates her account to use a pen name? In plain JavaScript, you are forced to write manual commands to find and rewrite every single spot. You need to hunt down each and every "name" variable, manually. If you miss in one place, it does not update. This is the problem with imperative programming: it is imperative to hunt down and update all variables, time and time again. Which, in turn, can lead to many silent failures. This silent failure is exactly why you need the declarative component model of React: it eliminates manual DOM hunting to ensure your entire interface stays perfectly synchronized automatically.

The Declarative Shift

React was created to eliminate this category of bugs entirely. Instead of forcing you to write imperative instructions that manually mutate individual browser elements, React introduces a declarative programming model (a design paradigm where you describe what the user interface should look like for a given state, rather than how to manipulate the screen step by step).

Key Takeaway

In imperative programming you describe how to update; in React you describe what to show.

When you write plain JavaScript DOM code, your script is an instruction manual for the browser: find this node, verify that it exists, overwrite its text, and attach an event listener. React reverses this relationship. Instead of telling the browser how to modify the document over time, you write a function that receives data and returns a declarative UI description of the completed interface. You provide the destination address, and React handles the underlying browser navigation.

Because your code only describes the finished screen for any given value, there is no list of manual DOM queries to maintain. If the reader's name changes from Elena to her new pen name, you do not hunt down ten DOM elements. You simply supply the new name to React. React evaluates your description, calculates the difference, and updates every visible spot on the screen through automated state synchronization.

Components as Reusable Blueprints

In plain HTML, you structure documents using native HTML tags like <header>, <article>, and <button>. However, native HTML tags do not know anything about your application logic, your subscriber tiers, or your reader data. Traditionally, developers had to copy and paste chunks of HTML structure across templates and attach separate JavaScript scripts to add behavior.

To solve this fragmentation, React combines markup, style, and logic into a single cohesive structure. This mechanism is called a component (a self-contained, reusable JavaScript function that accepts data inputs called props and returns markup describing a piece of the user interface).

In React, every component is a standard JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter. Capitalization is a strict requirement: it tells React that <SiteHeader /> is your custom component, whereas <header> is a built-in browser DOM tag. Components can be nested inside one another, allowing you to assemble complex pages out of small, focused building blocks.

To see this in action on The National Times, we can organize our site header into three distinct files. The parent component SiteHeader.jsx acts as the container. Inside it, we place two specialized child components: ReaderGreeting.jsx, which renders the welcome message, and SubscriberInfo.jsx, which renders the subscriber profile details. Both child components receive readerName as an input prop from their parent.

    • SiteHeader.jsx
    • SubscriberInfo.jsx

<ReaderGreeting readerName={readerName} />
<SubscriberInfo readerName={readerName} />

The component explorer panel above illustrates this relationship. On the left, the file hierarchy shows SiteHeader.jsx containing both ReaderGreeting.jsx and SubscriberInfo.jsx. On the right, the rendered canvas displays the final visual output: the greeting box displays "Welcome back, Morgan", while the subscriber info displays "Subscriber: Morgan" alongside the subscription plan. The reader name "Morgan" flows directly from the parent container into both child components. Neither child queries the DOM; each merely returns a declarative description of its own HTML elements.

Let us look closely at how our first child component, ReaderGreeting.jsx, receives and projects this data:

ReaderGreeting.jsx
1export default function ReaderGreeting({ readerName }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="greeting-box">
4 <span>Welcome back, {readerName}</span>
Projects reader name directly into MARKUP
5 </div>
6 );
7}

The component function ReaderGreeting receives its input data through a single parameter called props (short for properties). Rather than writing props.readerName throughout the function body, the signature uses JavaScript object destructuring directly inside the parentheses: ({ readerName }). This unpacks the readerName property straight into a local variable. Inside the markup, the curly braces around {readerName} establish an evaluation window that steps out of static HTML structure and into live JavaScript execution. When React evaluates this component, it reads the current value of readerName and projects it straight into the text content of the span, eliminating manual string concatenation and DOM lookups.

Our second child component, SubscriberInfo.jsx, follows the same pattern to assemble a subscriber card:

SubscriberInfo.jsx
1export default function SubscriberInfo({ readerName }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="subscriber-info">
4 <p className="user-name">Subscriber: {readerName}</p>
Reflects the current prop VALUE
5 <p className="user-status">Plan: All-Access</p>
Static metadata stays UNCHANGED
6 </div>
7 );
8}

The implementation of SubscriberInfo demonstrates how dynamic expressions and static markup coexist harmoniously within a single component. The paragraph rendering {readerName} recalculates dynamically whenever incoming props change, whereas the adjacent paragraph displaying Plan: All-Access remains completely static. React compiles both elements into a single declarative blueprint, ensuring that styling and structural scaffolding remain untouched while only the dynamic tokens update in response to fresh data.

With both child components prepared, SiteHeader.jsx imports them and assembles the completed site header:

SiteHeader.jsx
1import ReaderGreeting from './ReaderGreeting.jsx';
2import SubscriberInfo from './SubscriberInfo.jsx';
3
4export default function SiteHeader({ readerName }) {
5 return (
6 <header className="site-header">
7 <h1>The National Times</h1>
Brand heading declared STATICALLY
8 <div className="header-actions">
9 <ReaderGreeting readerName={readerName} />
Passes reader name to GREETING
10 <SubscriberInfo readerName={readerName} />
Passes same reader name to SUBSCRIBER
11 </div>
12 </header>
13 );
14}

The container SiteHeader orchestrates child components through the contract of prop passing: <ReaderGreeting readerName={readerName} /> Notice the two distinct halves of this JSX attribute. The left side, readerName=, defines the property name expected by the child component, while the right side within curly braces, ={readerName}, supplies the parent component's live variable. Through this downward flow, SiteHeader distributes its data cleanly to both child components without either child needing to know where that data originated.

This composition also exposes the foundational distinction between HTML elements and custom React components. When React encounters lowercase tags like <header>, <h1>, and <div>, it instructs the browser engine to instantiate native DOM elements. When it encounters capitalized tags like <ReaderGreeting /> and <SubscriberInfo />, it recognizes custom component functions, invokes them in memory, and stitches their returned UI descriptors into the render tree.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why do multi-component screens fall out of sync? What happens when a shopper clicks "Add to Cart" on a flash sale product? The slide-out drawer pops open and shows 3 items. But what about the checkout counter in the top navigation bar? It still says 2. Why? Because the manual script forgot to update the header counter. One variable in memory, two different numbers on the screen. This is split-brain state divergence. React eliminates this headache entirely. Instead of updating elements one by one, you pass the data down from a single source of truth. Because every component reads from that same single source of truth, every section on the screen updates together. Instantly.

How React Synchronizes the Screen

If our component functions never touch the browser DOM, how does the screen actually change when application data updates? A naive alternative approach would be to destroy the existing container markup and recreate the entire HTML subtree from scratch on every change. However, tearing down physical DOM elements produces catastrophic side effects: active input fields lose keyboard focus, ongoing CSS transitions cancel abruptly, and browser performance degrades under continuous layout recalculation.

React avoids this destruction through an intelligent comparison pipeline. When a component executes, React constructs an in-memory tree of lightweight JavaScript objects representing the intended user interface structure, known classically as the virtual DOM (and referred to in modern React documentation as a UI descriptor tree). When data updates, React runs the component again to produce a new virtual DOM tree. It then diffs the new tree against the previous tree through a process called reconciliation (the comparison algorithm React uses to compute the minimal set of physical DOM mutations required to bring the screen into alignment).

During reconciliation of our National Times header, React observes that the parent <header>, the brand <h1>, and the surrounding container elements have identical types and positions. React leaves those physical DOM nodes completely untouched. It surgically patches only the specific text content nodes inside ReaderGreeting.jsx and SubscriberInfo.jsx that reflect the updated readerName. Because the physical elements stay in place, your page remains stable, responsive, and free from flickering.

⚡ IN THE WILD

What is the problem with updating the physical DOM? Can you imagine a routine update of the DOM while you are typing in a form? The container is destroyed and instantly rebuilt. Remember the blinking cursor that appears when completing a form? Well... it vanishes completely, and your next few keystrokes disappear into thin air. React prevents this frustrating wipeout entirely. Instead of destroying the physical DOM, it compares the new updates in memory (the virtual DOM) and only touches the real physical DOM when changes are absolutely necessary, leaving your active typing perfectly untouched.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked why declarative UI beats manual DOM scripting, do not just say "it is easier to write." Explain the predictability of state synchronization: manual DOM scripting distributes state across two places, namely your JavaScript variables and the live DOM nodes. React eliminates that split by making the DOM a pure projection of data, so your screen and your data can never drift apart.

Where you will meet this

  • News site header user profiles: updating a subscriber name or tier immediately syncs the top navigation, the comment author label, and the sidebar subscriber profile without querying element IDs.
  • E-commerce shopping carts: clicking an item count button updates the cart flyout total, the header item counter, and the checkout summary from a single data source.
  • Live match scoreboards: updating a team score increments the main score banner, the mini score display, and the box score simultaneously without DOM queries.

Glossary

  • Declarative Programming: A programming model where you describe what the user interface should look like for a given state without writing manual step-by-step browser commands.
  • Imperative DOM Scripting: A programming style where you write explicit, manual instructions commanding the browser how to locate and mutate individual DOM nodes.
  • State Drift: The divergence where computer memory holds updated data, but the live webpage still renders stale or partial content.
  • Component: A self-contained, reusable JavaScript function that accepts data inputs called props and returns markup describing a piece of the user interface.
  • Virtual DOM: An in-memory tree of lightweight JavaScript objects representing the intended user interface structure used by React to calculate differences.
  • Reconciliation: The comparison algorithm React uses to diff the virtual DOM against the previous render and compute the minimal set of physical DOM mutations.

Summary

Declarative State Projections vs Imperative DOM Mutations

In daily production, choosing between imperative DOM manipulation and declarative React components defines how you structure user interfaces. While manual scripting requires micromanaging every element update, React lets you declare the desired target state and handles the mutations automatically. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ Imperative versus Declarative Mental Models
  1. Avoid manual DOM queries and imperative mutations to keep state synchronized across your interface.
        (a) Manually querying elements and mutating properties leads to state drift and broken references when IDs change.
        (b) Declare UI as a pure projection of data, letting React handle DOM updates when inputs change.
  2. Prevent state divergence by maintaining a single declarative source of truth.
        (a) Storing state across multiple disparate DOM elements requires synchronized manual mutations that easily fail.
        (b) Pass state into reusable component blueprints that recalculate their output automatically.

➔ NEVER query or mutate physical DOM nodes manually inside React applications.

➔ ALWAYS declare the target UI state and let React reconcile changes to the real DOM.

➔ IF multiple interface elements depend on the same data THEN project that data through declarative component props.

DO THIS: Author clean, declarative React components that accept props and project data directly into JSX without manual DOM mutations.

ReaderGreeting.jsx
1export default function ReaderGreeting({ readerName }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="greeting-box">
4 <span>Welcome back, {readerName}</span>
5 </div>
6 );
7}

DO NOT DO THIS: Never write manual DOM queries, null checks, or imperative mutations to update UI text in application scripts.

Manual DOM Script

2 const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting-text');
3 if (greeting) greeting.textContent = `Welcome back, ${newName}`;
4 const tag = document.getElementById('subscriber-tag');
5 if (tag) tag.textContent = `Subscriber: ${newName}`;
6}

Lecture 2: Creating a Project: Framework versus Build Tool

Interview Question

CORE

How do you create and run a new React project, and how do you choose between a framework and a build tool?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. A developer named Marcus prepares to build a weather report for The National Times website.
  2. Marcus opens his terminal program to run the command that creates the project.
  3. The official documentation recommends a framework, but an online tutorial suggests a simple build tool.
  4. Which command should Marcus run in his terminal to start the project?
  5. Choosing the wrong tool forces him to rewrite routing and data loading weeks into production.
  6. Both tools create working pages, but they run code and handle data in completely different places.
  7. Today you learn the exact terminal commands to start a project and how to choose between them.

The Modern Starting Point

When you start a modern React application today, you cannot simply link a JavaScript file inside an HTML document. React components rely on JSX syntax and modular imports across multiple files. Browsers cannot execute raw JSX directly. Your development environment requires specialized tooling to compile your code, resolve dependencies, and prepare your project for deployment.

Choosing how to start a project requires making an early architectural choice between a build tool and a framework. A build tool (a command-line development program that compiles, bundles, and serves application code for browser execution) packages your source files into optimized JavaScript. The modern standard for standalone client projects is Vite. In contrast, a framework (an integrated application architecture that manages routing, data loading, and server execution) runs your code across both the server and the browser. Prominent examples include Next.js and React Router v7.

This choice directly determines your application's rendering strategy. A standalone build tool uses client-side rendering (CSR), delivering an empty HTML shell and running all React logic inside the user's browser. A full-stack framework unlocks server-side rendering (SSR), where React runs on a server to generate full HTML on each request, as well as static-site generation (SSG), where HTML is pre-rendered at build time.

Historically, the default starting tool was Create React App. However, Create React App is officially deprecated and unmaintained. It relied on monolithic Webpack builds that grew painfully slow as applications scaled, and it offered no architecture for modern server-rendered React features. Today, every new project starts either with a dedicated build tool like Vite or an integrated framework.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why did Create React App get retired? In older React projects, saving a single file forced the computer to rebuild your entire application from scratch. Developers regularly waited twenty seconds for the local development server to recompile. As projects grew larger, the browser was forced to download massive files before displaying a single pixel on screen. This is the problem with older bundlers: they force the user to wait for giant bundles, time and time again. A modern build tool like Vite eliminates this delay by serving individual files over native browser modules. A modern framework eliminates the blank screen by pre-rendering HTML on the server.

Generating a Project with Vite

When your application does not require a backend server or complex search engine optimization, the fastest path to production is a modern build tool. The standard choice recommended across the React ecosystem is Vite. Vite provides instant local startup and near-instant updates during development.

To create a new project, developers use a command-line scaffolding tool. In documentation, this command is described using a generic formula: npm create vite@latest <app_name> -- --template react In this generic formula, the token <app_name> represents a placeholder for your chosen application name. In practice, this value determines the physical folder created on your hard drive, as well as the "name" property recorded inside your package.json manifest. You must follow standard package naming rules: use lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens without spaces or uppercase characters, such as national-weather. Notice the angle brackets <...>: in command-line documentation, angle brackets denote a required parameter that you replace with your own value. You must never type the literal angle brackets into your terminal, because shells like bash and zsh treat < and > as file redirection operators, which trigger immediate syntax errors.

Notice also the tool invocation flags. The command npm create vite@latest is shorthand for npm exec create-vite@latest. It downloads the latest create-vite scaffolding package into temporary cache, executes it in memory, and cleans it up without leaving an unmaintained global program on your computer. The double-dash delimiter -- is mandatory: npm consumes all arguments before the double-dash, while everything placed after -- is forwarded directly to the underlying create-vite program. Without that delimiter, npm attempts to interpret --template react as an internal npm flag and aborts. The --template react argument instructs the generator to scaffold a React project pre-configured for standard JavaScript and JSX.

Here is the concrete runnable command sequence to generate and start your project:

Terminal
1npm create vite@latest national-weather -- --template react
1. scaffolds the PROJECT directory
2cd national-weather
2. navigates into the project DIRECTORY
3npm install
3. installs the React DEPENDENCIES
4npm run dev
4. starts the local DEVELOPMENT server

After running the scaffolding command, Vite generates a clean, purposeful project structure on your hard drive. It is essential to understand the exact role of each generated file and folder:

  • index.html: Unlike older tooling that hid the HTML entry point inside a public/ directory, Vite places index.html directly at the root of your project. It serves as the true entry point of the application, defining the container <div id="root"></div> and loading your source code through a native browser module tag: <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
  • package.json: The central project manifest. It records your project name, declares runtime dependencies (react and react-dom), lists development dependencies (vite and the @vitejs/plugin-react compiler plugin), and defines runnable scripts such as npm run dev and npm run build.
  • vite.config.js: The central configuration file for the build tool. It registers the official @vitejs/plugin-react plugin. This plugin connects three critical tools:
    • JSX compilation: Browsers cannot read JSX tags like <WeatherReport />. The compiler transforms these tags into standard JavaScript function calls that any browser engine can run.
    • Fast Refresh: When you edit component code during development, this tool updates only that component in browser memory within milliseconds. It preserves your existing state, such as text typed into input boxes, without reloading the webpage.
    • Rollup bundling: When you prepare your application for production, Rollup bundles your dozens of separate source files. It deletes unused code and compresses everything into a few small, highly optimized files ready for deployment.
  • src/: The directory where your actual application code lives. Inside it, main.jsx imports React DOM, selects the #root element, and mounts your component tree. Beside it, App.jsx serves as your root component, while index.css and App.css supply baseline layout styles.

Following scaffolding, running cd national-weather enters the project folder, where npm install reads package.json to download the dependencies into the newly created node_modules/ folder. This installation step also produces package-lock.json, which locks the exact resolved version of every package to guarantee reproducible builds across developer machines. Finally, running npm run dev starts the local development server, typically at http://localhost:5173.

When you edit files inside this running project, Vite updates the screen almost instantaneously. It achieves this through Hot Module Replacement (a development mechanism that replaces only the edited component in browser memory without reloading the entire webpage). Because the webpage never refreshes completely, your active component memory and scroll position remain undisturbed.

To examine what Vite generates out of the box, we inspect the default project structure. Inside the src/ directory, Vite creates App.jsx, which serves as the canonical starter component:

national-weather — Component Explorer

    • App.jsx

On the right, the rendered canvas displays the starter interface: the heading "Vite + React", an interactive counter button showing "count is 0", and the helper caption "Click button to increment count".

Here is the exact code generated inside App.jsx:

App.jsx
1import { useState } from 'react';
2
3export default function App() {
4 const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
5 return (
6 <div className="card">
7 <div className="starter-heading">Vite + React</div>

10 </button>

12 </div>

14}

The starter component App.jsx imports useState from React to equip the component with internal state memory. Calling useState(0) initializes a reactive counter to zero, returning the current count value alongside its dedicated setter setCount. Inside the rendered button, the JSX expression {count} reads this state variable directly. When the user clicks the button, the inline onClick callback invokes setCount((c) => c + 1) React updates the state variable in memory, re-evaluates the component function, and reconciles the button text from 0 to 1 without touching the heading or surrounding layout.

⚡ IN THE WILD

What makes a modern build tool so fast? In older bundlers, saving a single file forced the tool to repackage every file in the project into one gigantic bundle before the browser could see the change. A modern build tool like Vite works completely differently. When you edit a component, the development server transforms only that single file and sends it directly to the browser. Your browser requests only what changed, time and time again. Because the server never re-bundles the entire codebase, updates happen in milliseconds through Hot Module Replacement. In this mechanism, the development server keeps a live connection to your browser. When you save a file, the server sends the updated module directly over this connection. The browser swaps the new code into memory instantly and re-renders the component, so you see your changes immediately without losing your current form inputs or scroll position.

Client-Side Rendering Mechanics

Understanding Vite requires understanding the physical network reality of client-side rendering (CSR). When a visitor opens your website in their browser, the web server does not send a completed HTML document. Instead, the server delivers an almost empty HTML file:

code.txt
1<!doctype html>
2<html lang="en">
3 <body>
4 <div id="root"></div>
5 <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
6 </body>
7</html>

Notice what is missing from this HTML: there are no headlines, no paragraphs, and no weather forecasts. The body contains only an empty root container <div id="root"></div> and a script tag. In the classic industry lexicon, this architecture is known as a Single-Page Application (SPA). In the modern React specification, this structure represents a client-rendered UI descriptor tree.

Once the browser downloads this HTML document, it encounters the script tag. The browser then makes a second network request to fetch the compiled JavaScript bundle. Only after that JavaScript bundle arrives does the browser execute React in local CPU memory. React evaluates your components, builds the in-memory tree, and inserts the resulting DOM nodes into the empty root container.

This sequence reveals the core architectural trade-off of client-side rendering:

  • Instant Client Transitions: Once the application is loaded into browser memory, clicking between views or updating components is instantaneous. The browser never makes another full page request.
  • Cheap Static Hosting: Because the server only delivers static HTML, JavaScript, and CSS files, you can host the application on any global Content Delivery Network without managing backend servers.
  • The Initial Blank Screen: The browser cannot display anything until the full JavaScript bundle downloads and executes. On slow cellular connections, visitors stare at a blank white screen during initial loading.
  • Search Engine Limitations: Search engine crawlers and social media preview bots may read the initial empty HTML before JavaScript executes, making search indexation unpredictable.

⚡ IN THE WILD

When does client-side rendering show a white screen? Imagine a reader on a mobile phone opens The National Times. The screen stays completely blank for several seconds before anything appears. This delay happens because the server sends an empty HTML document with nothing more than an empty root container. The browser cannot display a single headline or button until it finishes downloading and executing the entire JavaScript bundle. On a slow mobile network, the reader stares at this blank screen while waiting for the code to arrive. This initial delay is the fundamental cost of client-side rendering: the user must download the full application engine before seeing any content.

When to Choose a Full-Stack Framework

A framework expands beyond file compilation to provide a complete software architecture. While a build tool leaves page routing, data fetching patterns, and server deployment entirely to the developer, a framework integrates these responsibilities into a cohesive system.

To generate a project using a full-stack framework, you use the framework's official scaffolding CLI:

Terminal
1npx create-next-app@latest national-times-web
Next.js full-stack framework
2npx create-react-router@latest national-portal
React Router full-stack framework

Full-stack frameworks solve the initial white screen problem through server-side rendering (SSR). When a reader requests a web page, the server executes the React component functions immediately on its own CPU. The server outputs fully constructed HTML containing real text and markup. The server streams that HTML to the browser across the network.

The browser displays this HTML immediately. The reader sees headlines, articles, and weather forecasts without waiting for JavaScript. While the reader reads the content, the browser downloads the JavaScript bundle in the background. Once the JavaScript arrives, it attaches event listeners to the existing HTML in a process called hydration (the process where client-side React attaches event handlers to pre-rendered server HTML).

Frameworks also provide static-site generation (SSG). For pages that do not change on every incoming request, the framework runs your React components once during your deployment build. The framework exports pre-rendered HTML files that can be stored on edge servers worldwide.

Here is the senior engineering decision matrix for choosing your starting foundation:

  1. Choose a Build Tool (Vite) when:
  • You are building an internal company dashboard, admin portal, or authenticated account tool behind a login.
  • Search engine optimization is unnecessary because the application is private.
  • You want zero backend infrastructure, hosting purely on static file storage.
  • You are learning core React fundamentals, testing an isolated component, or building a lightweight client tool.
  1. Choose a Full-Stack Framework (Next.js or React Router) when:
  • You are building a public-facing website, e-commerce catalog, or news publication where fast first-contentful paint and search engine visibility are critical.
  • The application contains dozens of distinct pages requiring automatic code splitting and nested routing.
  • You want to query databases directly from server components without writing separate REST API endpoints.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Does a full-stack framework require a backend server? Many developers avoid frameworks because they fear the operational burden of managing backend servers. But modern frameworks support static exports. They can generate pre-rendered HTML files during the build and upload them straight to a static file host. You do not need a running server. This means you can use a framework purely for its routing and pre-rendering capabilities without maintaining any server infrastructure.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked whether to use Next.js or Vite, never offer an opinionated preference. Frame your answer around architectural constraints. Explain that Vite provides simplicity, complete architectural control, and zero server maintenance for client-focused applications. Explain that a framework provides built-in routing, server-rendered HTML for search engines, and integrated data loading at the cost of framework conventions and hosting requirements.

Where you will meet this

  • Internal newsroom dashboard: building a live weather monitoring tool inside an authenticated employee portal using Vite for rapid client compilation.
  • Public news article page: publishing breaking news stories using Next.js with static-site generation so millions of global readers receive cached HTML instantly.
  • Subscriber account portal: managing billing preferences and credit card updates using React Router with server-side data loaders to keep payment tokens secure.
  • Standalone interactive calculator: compiling a loan payment calculator into a client-only bundle with Vite to embed inside third-party partner websites.

Glossary

  • Build Tool: A command-line program that compiles source files, bundles dependencies, and serves local development assets for browser execution.
  • Full-Stack Framework: An integrated application architecture that manages routing, server-side data loading, and execution across both server and browser environments.
  • Client-Side Rendering (CSR): A rendering architecture where the server delivers a minimal HTML shell and the browser executes JavaScript to construct the user interface.
  • Server-Side Rendering (SSR): A rendering architecture where the web server runs React components on each HTTP request to generate and send fully constructed HTML to the browser.
  • Hydration: The client-side process where React attaches event listeners to pre-rendered server HTML to make the static markup interactive.
  • Hot Module Replacement (HMR): A development mechanism that replaces updated component modules in browser memory over a live connection without reloading the full page.

Summary

Build Tools versus Full-Stack Frameworks

In daily production, choosing between a build tool and a full-stack framework establishes the architectural foundation of your application. While a build tool focuses strictly on compiling client-side JavaScript, a framework provides an integrated platform managing the entire request lifecycle. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ Client Bundling versus Server-Integrated Platforms
  1. Choose a build tool like Vite when building client-focused applications that do not require server execution.
        (a) Vite compiles JSX and bundles assets with near-instant local server startup.
        (b) Delivers an empty HTML shell that executes all React logic in browser memory via client-side rendering.
  2. Choose a full-stack framework like Next.js or React Router when building public web applications requiring search visibility and fast initial loads.
        (a) Pre-renders HTML on the server or during build time to eliminate initial blank screens.
        (b) Provides built-in file-based routing, server data loaders, and automatic code splitting.

➔ NEVER deploy a public, content-heavy application using pure client-side rendering if search engine optimization matters.

➔ ALWAYS use a modern build tool like Vite for authenticated dashboards, prototypes, and isolated client components.

➔ IF your application requires fast initial paint and multi-route navigation THEN choose an integrated full-stack framework.

DO THIS: Pre-render public content on the server or at build time so search crawlers and readers receive full HTML immediately.

4 <h1>{article.title}</h1>
5 <p className="story-lead">{article.lead}</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

Lecture 3: Component Anatomy: Functions, Capitalization, and Declarations

Interview Question

CORE

What is a React component, and what rules govern how you write and name one?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. A web developer named Leo builds an author card for The National Times.
  2. Leo writes a JavaScript function named authorProfile to display the writer's name.
  3. He adds the lowercase tag to the page and runs the development server.
  4. Why does the browser show a blank space instead of the author's card?
  5. Missing author cards confuse readers and leave journalists without credit for breaking stories.
  6. The function returns valid markup, but the compiler treats lowercase names as browser tags.
  7. Today you learn how capitalization dictates component identity and why case rules matter.

What is a React Component?

In traditional web development, building an interface required juggling three separate technologies across different files. Developers wrote page structure in HTML, visual rules in CSS, and dynamic behavior in JavaScript. As web applications grew into rich interactive experiences, this separation created severe maintenance friction: changing a single button required opening three files and hoping the class names and DOM queries stayed synchronized.

React solves this fragmentation by uniting markup, design, and logic into cohesive, self-contained units called components. A component (known classically as a React Component and in modern documentation as a Function Component) is a regular JavaScript function that returns a user interface description written in JSX. Rather than writing an imperative sequence of browser commands, you author a function that defines what a piece of the screen should look like.

Under the hood, a component is not a heavy object-oriented class, nor is it a native browser Web Component. In computer memory, it is simply a plain JavaScript function that returns a lightweight object descriptor. When React renders your application, it invokes your component function, captures the returned UI descriptor tree, and coordinates with the browser engine to paint the real DOM nodes on the screen.

⚡ IN THE WILD

What is a React component under the hood? You look at <AuthorProfile /> on your screen and wonder what wizardry created it. Is it a complex browser extension or a heavy object class? In reality, it is nothing more than a plain JavaScript function. React executes that function and gets back a plain JavaScript object. It is a plain function returning a plain object, time and time again. This simplicity is the secret to React. Because every component is just a plain JavaScript function, React can run it, test it, and evaluate its UI descriptor in memory at lightning speed without touching the slow physical DOM until the exact moment of rendering.

The Capitalization Law: Why Case Dictates DOM Identity

Because components are standard JavaScript functions, beginners often assume they can name them using standard camelCase conventions, such as function authorProfile() However, React enforces an ironclad syntactic rule: every component name must begin with a capital letter using PascalCase.

This requirement exists because the JSX compiler needs a fast, unambiguous mechanism to differentiate between native HTML elements and custom user-defined components. When the compiler parses your JSX markup, it examines the first letter of each tag name. If the tag begins with a lowercase letter, such as <header>, <p>, or <authorProfile />, the compiler outputs a string literal: _jsx('authorProfile', {}). When React encounters a string tag name, it instructs the browser to create a native DOM node with that exact tag name.

When Leo named his component authorProfile with a lowercase a, the browser searched its internal HTML registry for a tag named <authorprofile>. Finding no standard element matching that name, the browser rendered an empty, inert custom HTML element. Leo's JavaScript function was never invoked, its internal JSX was never evaluated, and the author's name was completely omitted from the rendered page.

Key Takeaway

In JSX, lowercase means a real browser tag; uppercase means a React component function.

If you capitalize the first letter and write <AuthorProfile />, the compiler behavior changes completely. Because the tag begins with an uppercase letter, the compiler treats AuthorProfile as a direct JavaScript identifier rather than a string: _jsx(AuthorProfile, {}). React receives the actual function reference and executes AuthorProfile() directly, evaluating its returned markup and mounting the author profile to the document.

To see this architectural contract in practice, examine how The National Times structures its article header. The parent container ArticleHeader.jsx imports and renders our presentation child component AuthorProfile.jsx:

national-times — Component Explorer
Project Files
  • components
    • ArticleHeader.jsx
    • AuthorProfile.jsx
ArticleHeader
AuthorProfile
Written by Elena VanceColumnist, Metro Desk

The component explorer panel above demonstrates this structure. On the left, the file hierarchy shows ArticleHeader.jsx serving as the parent container, with AuthorProfile.jsx nested inside. On the right, the rendered canvas displays the completed output: "Written by Elena Vance" above her editorial role "Columnist, Metro Desk". The child component encapsulates the author's credentials into a reusable blueprint that can be embedded across any article template.

Here is the implementation of our child component, AuthorProfile.jsx:

AuthorProfile.jsx
1export default function AuthorProfile() {
2 return (
3 <div className="profile-box">
4 <p className="profile-name">Written by Elena Vance</p>
Capitalized component returns author NAME
5 <span className="profile-role">Columnist, Metro Desk</span>
Editorial role rendered in SPAN
6 </div>
7 );
8}

The component function AuthorProfile begins with a capital A. Following PascalCase naming satisfies the compiler gate, allowing other files to import and render this function as a first-class component. Marking the declaration with export default establishes AuthorProfile as the primary export of the file, enabling parent components to bring it into scope cleanly.

Inside the return statement, AuthorProfile returns a <div> containing a <p> and a <span>. Because these tags are written entirely in lowercase, React translates them into standard browser DOM nodes (HTMLDivElement, HTMLParagraphElement, and HTMLSpanElement). The component packages both the structural layout and the static author text into a single reusable unit.

Now let us examine how the parent container, ArticleHeader.jsx, renders this child component:

ArticleHeader.jsx
1import AuthorProfile from './AuthorProfile.jsx';
2
3export default function ArticleHeader() {
4 return (
5 <header className="article-header">
6 <h1 className="story-title">Mayoral Election Special Report</h1>
Native lowercase h1 renders directly to DOM
7 <div className="header-meta">
8 <AuthorProfile />
Capitalized tag invokes AuthorProfile component FUNCTION
9 </div>
10 </header>
11 );
12}

Notice the stark contrast between the tags rendered inside ArticleHeader. The <header>, <h1>, and <div> tags begin with lowercase letters, so React emits them directly as native browser elements. In contrast, <AuthorProfile /> begins with an uppercase letter. React recognizes that AuthorProfile is a custom component, resolves the imported function identifier, and invokes AuthorProfile() to collect its rendered output.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does capitalization change how code runs? In standard JavaScript, writing a lowercase function name works identically to an uppercase name. But in JSX, capitalization is an ironclad compiler law. If you type <authorProfile />, the compiler treats it as a built-in browser element. If you type <AuthorProfile />, the compiler treats it as your custom component function. This single capital letter decides whether React invokes your function or sends an unknown string to the browser. By enforcing capitalization through PascalCase, React separates native browser tags from your custom component functions cleanly.

Return Rules: Parentheses and Automatic Semicolon Insertion

Every React component function must return something that React can render, such as JSX markup, a string, a number, or null. When returning JSX that spans multiple lines, you must follow an essential syntactic rule: always wrap multi-line JSX markup in parentheses.

To understand why parentheses are mandatory, you must understand how the JavaScript engine reads your code. JavaScript features a compiler mechanism called Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI). If you place a line break immediately after the return keyword without an opening parenthesis, JavaScript assumes you intended to write a standalone return statement and automatically inserts an invisible semicolon: return;.

When ASI triggers on an unparenthesized return statement, your component function terminates immediately after the return keyword, returning undefined. The JavaScript engine never reads the subsequent JSX markup. When React receives undefined from a component render, it throws a runtime crash: Nothing was returned from render Wrapping the return statement in opening and closing parentheses return (...) prevents ASI by signaling to JavaScript that the expression continues across line breaks.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does returning on a newline fail? You hit Enter after typing return to keep your code tidy and readable. On the next line, you start your JSX markup. You save the file, and your browser screen crashes with a blank error. Why? Because the JavaScript language inserts a hidden semicolon right after the word return. Your function ends immediately. It returns undefined, and your entire component is completely ignored. This is the silent trap of Automatic Semicolon Insertion: hitting Enter cuts off your return statement before it ever reaches your markup. Wrapping your code in parentheses keeps the statement open and safe.

The Anti-Nesting Law: Never Define Components Inside Components

As your application grows, you will frequently assemble components out of smaller sub-components. However, there is a fundamental difference between component composition (rendering one component inside another) and nested component definitions (declaring the function body of a child component inside the function body of a parent component).

You must never define a component function inside another component function:

ArticleHeader.jsx
1export default function ArticleHeader() {
2 function AuthorProfile() {
3 return <p className="profile-name">Written by Elena Vance</p>;
WRONG: re-allocated on every parent RENDER
4 }
5 return (
6 <header>
7 <AuthorProfile />
8 </header>
9 );
10}

The code above appears harmless to developers accustomed to nesting helper functions in plain JavaScript. In React, however, this pattern triggers severe performance degradation and catastrophic state bugs. Every time ArticleHeader renders, JavaScript allocates a brand new AuthorProfile function in memory with a completely new function reference.

When React reconciles the user interface, it compares the type of each component against the previous render. Because the nested AuthorProfile function has a fresh memory address on every render cycle, React assumes that the old component was deleted and a completely different component was inserted in its place. React destroys the entire existing DOM subtree, discards all internal state, wipes user form inputs, resets scroll positions, and mounts a brand new DOM element from scratch.

To preserve component identity across renders, always declare every component function at the top level of the file. When a child component requires data from its parent, pass that data downward through props rather than nesting function declarations.

⚡ IN THE WILD

When does nested code destroy your state? You might think declaring a helper component inside your main component keeps your file organized. It looks harmless. But every time the parent component re-renders, the computer creates a brand new function in memory. React looks at that new function, assumes it is a completely new component type, and tears down the entire DOM tree. Any input you typed vanishes instantly. This is the danger of nested component definitions: you recreate the component blueprint on every render, resetting state over and over again. Declaring your component at the top level keeps component identity stable.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked why nesting component definitions is an anti-pattern, do not just say "it hurts performance." Frame your answer around component identity and DOM mounting. Explain that React identifies components by function reference. Defining a component inside another re-allocates that function on every parent render, destroying component identity, wiping child component state, and forcing the browser to recreate DOM nodes unnecessarily.

Where you will meet this

  • Editorial author profiles on news articles: packaging author names, headshots, and editorial desks into reusable <AuthorProfile /> components across layout templates.
  • Standardized design system button libraries: creating customizable <Button /> components that encapsulate brand styling and click handlers across web applications.
  • Verified subscriber labels in community forums: rendering authenticated subscriber tags next to reader comments without duplicating markup or styles.
  • Video player media controls: encapsulating play, pause, and scrub bar functionality inside dedicated player components on streaming portals.

Glossary

  • Component: A self-contained, reusable JavaScript function that begins with a capital letter and returns a user interface description in JSX.
  • PascalCase: The naming convention where the first letter of every word is capitalized, required for all React component function names.
  • Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI): The JavaScript parser mechanism that automatically inserts semicolons at line breaks, requiring parentheses around multi-line return statements.
  • Component Identity: The persistent reference React uses to track a component across renders, preserved only when the component is declared at the top level.
  • UI Descriptor Tree: An in-memory hierarchy of lightweight JavaScript objects generated by JSX that describes the intended DOM structure to React.

Summary

Component Anatomy: Functions, Capitalization, and Declarations

In daily production, understanding component anatomy ensures that your user interface blueprints render reliably and maintain predictable lifecycle behavior. While plain JavaScript functions execute arbitrary calculations, React component functions serve as declarative factories producing user interface descriptors. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ Capitalization Rules and Component Identity
  1. Enforce PascalCase capitalization on all component declarations to ensure correct JSX compilation.
        (a) Lowercase tags compile into string literals that instruct the browser to render native HTML elements.
        (b) Uppercase tags compile into function identifiers that instruct React to execute your custom component code.
  2. Preserve component identity across render cycles by declaring all components at the top level.
        (a) Nesting component definitions inside other functions re-allocates the child function on every render.
        (b) Declaring components at the top level prevents unnecessary DOM destruction and avoids state wipeouts.

➔ NEVER define a component function inside another component function.

➔ ALWAYS capitalize the first letter of every component name using PascalCase.

➔ IF returning multi-line JSX THEN wrap the entire return expression in parentheses.

DO THIS: Declare component functions at the top level using PascalCase and wrap multi-line JSX in parentheses.

AuthorProfile.jsx
1export default function AuthorProfile() {
2 return (
3 <div className="profile-box">
4 <p className="profile-name">Written by Elena Vance</p>
5 </div>
6 );
7}

DO NOT DO THIS: Never define component functions inside other components or return multi-line JSX without parentheses.

ArticleHeader.jsx
1export default function ArticleHeader() {
2 function AuthorProfile() {
3 return <p className="profile-name">Written by Elena Vance</p>;
4 }
5 return <header><AuthorProfile /></header>;
6}

Lecture 4: JSX Syntax Rules and Fragment Architecture

Interview Question

CORE

What is JSX, what syntax rules must every snippet follow, and how do Fragments group elements without wrapper nodes?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. A developer named Marcus migrates an article summary into a new component for The National Times.
  2. He pastes standard HTML containing two sibling paragraphs and an unclosed image tag into the file.
  3. Marcus saves the file and starts the development server to preview the article.
  4. Why does the compiler crash with a syntax error instead of showing the page?
  5. Build crashes halt daily publishing and prevent breaking stories from reaching readers.
  6. The markup is valid in a browser, but the JSX compiler strictly rejects it.
  7. Today you learn the syntax rules of JSX and how Fragments group elements cleanly.

Why JSX Is Not HTML

When developers first encounter React, JSX appears identical to traditional HTML. You write opening and closing angle brackets, assign attributes, and nest tags inside one another. However, this visual resemblance is misleading. JSX is not HTML, nor is it a raw text template parsed by the browser.

JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript (known classically as JSX / React Elements and in modern documentation as a JSX Syntax Extension / UI Descriptors). Under the hood, JSX provides a readable, declarative syntax that compilers like Vite, Babel, and SWC transform into standard JavaScript function calls. When you write <p className="lead">Breaking News</p> the compiler transforms that markup into _jsx('p', { className: 'lead', children: 'Breaking News' })

This transformation changes everything about how your code is evaluated. A web browser's HTML parser is intentionally permissive: if you forget to close an image tag or misplace an attribute, the browser forgives the error and renders whatever it can reconstruct. But JSX compiles directly into JavaScript objects and function arguments. JavaScript is a strict programming language that cannot tolerate missing commas, unclosed brackets, or invalid syntax. Because every JSX tag is a JavaScript function call in disguise, JSX enforces three strict syntax rules that every snippet must obey.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does valid HTML fail in JSX? In plain HTML, browsers are extremely forgiving. If you forget to close an image tag or type a class attribute, the browser forgives you and renders the page anyway. But JSX is not HTML. JSX is JavaScript in disguise. Every tag you write turns into a real JavaScript function call. A JavaScript function cannot accept broken syntax. It cannot have missing brackets or unclosed arguments. This is why JSX syntax is so strict: it compiles directly to JavaScript objects, where every single token must be valid code. Conforming to JSX syntax guarantees that your declarative markup transforms into valid JavaScript without compiler crashes.

Rule 1: The Single Root Rule and Fragment Architecture

The first universal rule of JSX is the single root rule: a component return statement or JSX expression must return exactly one root element. If you attempt to return two adjacent sibling elements side by side without an enclosing parent tag, the compiler throws an immediate syntax error.

To understand why this rule exists, look at the compiled JavaScript. When a function executes, JavaScript language grammar allows it to return exactly one value. Writing return <p>...</p> <span>...</span>; is equivalent to writing return _jsx('p'), _jsx('span'); In JavaScript, returning two separate objects from a single return statement is syntactically invalid. Every expression must resolve to a single value.

A common beginner reaction to this compiler constraint is wrapping everything in an extra <div>. While adding a wrapper div satisfies the compiler, it introduces a severe architectural defect known as wrapper div bloat (or "div soup"). Inserting unnecessary wrapper nodes pollutes the physical browser DOM, degrades accessibility tree navigation, and frequently breaks modern CSS layouts.

In CSS Grid and Flexbox, layout properties like display: flex, gap: 12px, and grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr) apply strictly to the container's direct children. If you insert an unnecessary wrapper <div> between a grid parent and its child elements, the browser treats the wrapper div as a single grid column, squishing all inner elements into that one column and destroying your design. Furthermore, inside strict HTML structures like <table>, wrapping multiple <td> table cells inside a <div> violates the HTML specification, causing browsers to eject the div entirely.

To solve this problem cleanly, React provides the Fragment (<>...</> or <React.Fragment>...</React.Fragment>). A Fragment is a built-in React component that lets you group multiple sibling elements together without injecting any physical wrapper node into the browser DOM tree.

To see how Fragments prevent layout breakage on The National Times, examine our article summary card. The parent component ArticleSummary.jsx renders an article tag using ArticleTag.jsx alongside story metadata rendered by StoryLead.jsx:

national-times — Component Explorer

On the right, the rendered canvas displays the completed card: an urgent tag reading "Special Investigation", directly followed by the lead text "City council votes on zoning." and the reading time "4 minute read". Neither child introduces unwanted wrapper divs.

Let us inspect our first child component, ArticleTag.jsx:

ArticleTag.jsx
1export default function ArticleTag() {
2 return (
3 <span className="tag-urgent">Special Investigation</span>
Single span returns inline TAG
4 );
5}

The ArticleTag component returns a single <span> element, naturally satisfying the single root rule without requiring an extra container div. It exports a focused inline tag component ready for composition.

Now examine our second child component, StoryLead.jsx, which must return two distinct sibling elements:

StoryLead.jsx
1export default function StoryLead() {
2 return (
3 <>
4 <p className="lead-text">City council votes on zoning.</p>
Fragment groups first sibling ELEMENT
5 <span className="read-time">4 minute read</span>
Fragment groups second sibling ELEMENT
6 </>
7 );
8}

Instead of wrapping the paragraph and span in an extra <div>, StoryLead encloses both siblings inside a Fragment (<>...</>). The JSX compiler recognizes the empty tags, groups both children into a single return expression, and attaches them directly to the parent layout without emitting an intermediate wrapper node into the DOM.

Now examine how the parent container, ArticleSummary.jsx, combines these components:

ArticleSummary.jsx
1import ArticleTag from './ArticleTag.jsx';
2import StoryLead from './StoryLead.jsx';

4export default function ArticleSummary() {
5 return (
6 <article className="summary-card">
7 <ArticleTag />
Renders article tag at top of CARD

9 </article>
10 );

When React mounts ArticleSummary, it evaluates StoryLead and attaches its inner <p> and <span> elements directly to the parent <article>. The browser DOM tree contains zero intermediate wrapper nodes.

⚡ IN THE WILD

When do extra divs break your layout? Imagine you configure a CSS grid with two equal columns. You place two elements inside a wrapper div to satisfy React's single root rule. Suddenly, your layout collapses. Why? Because CSS grid rules apply only to direct children. The browser sees your wrapper div as one single column instead of two independent items. This is the trap of wrapper div bloat: it inserts unwanted nodes into the DOM tree, breaking your grid and flexbox layouts. Using a Fragment (<>...</>) lets you return multiple sibling elements without rendering an extra node into the physical DOM tree, preserving your layout completely.

Rule 2: Explicit Tag Closure

The second universal rule of JSX is explicit tag closure: every single JSX tag must be closed explicitly. In traditional HTML, elements known as "void tags" (such as <img>, <input>,
, and <hr>) never have closing tags. Writing <img src="photo.jpg"> in standard HTML is completely valid.

In JSX, omitting the closing slash on any tag causes an immediate compiler crash. Void elements must be written as self-closing tags with a forward slash before the closing angle bracket: <img src="photo.jpg" /> <input type="text" /> and
. Wrapping tags that enclose children (such as <p> and <li>) must always include their corresponding closing tags (</p> and </li>).

This strictness is necessary because the JSX compiler processes your markup as an XML-like syntax tree. When the compiler encounters an unclosed tag, it cannot determine whether subsequent elements are children or siblings. Enforcing explicit closure ensures unambiguous syntax trees that translate cleanly into JavaScript objects.

Key Takeaway

In JSX, every tag must close and every snippet must share a single root.

Rule 3: camelCase Attributes and Reserved Words

The third universal rule of JSX governs attribute naming: most HTML and SVG attributes must be written in camelCase. Furthermore, certain standard HTML attribute names must be replaced to avoid collisions with JavaScript reserved words.

When the compiler transforms JSX into JavaScript, element attributes become property keys inside a plain JavaScript object. For example, <div id="banner"> compiles to _jsx('div', { id: 'banner' }) In JavaScript, object keys must follow language syntax rules. Words like class and for are reserved words in JavaScript: class creates object classes, and for creates loops.

To prevent syntax conflicts and maintain consistency with the browser's native DOM API, JSX introduces two critical attribute replacements:

  1. Use className instead of class. This matches the browser DOM property element.className.
  2. Use htmlFor instead of for. This matches the browser DOM property HTMLLabelElement.htmlFor.

Similarly, multi-word HTML and SVG attributes that use hyphens in standard HTML must be converted to camelCase attributes in JSX: stroke-width becomes strokeWidth, tabindex becomes tabIndex, and autocomplete becomes autoComplete.

There is one intentional exception to this rule: accessibility and custom data attributes remain hyphenated. Attributes prefixed with aria- (such as aria-label and aria-hidden) and data- (such as data-testid) are written with hyphens in JSX exactly as they are in HTML. The React team preserved this hyphenation to align directly with W3C accessibility and HTML specifications.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why do we write className instead of class? When developers first write JSX, typing className feels unnatural and irritating. Why can't we just write class? Because in JavaScript, the word class is already taken. It is a reserved keyword used to create JavaScript classes. When the compiler turns your JSX attributes into a JavaScript object, using reserved words can cause confusion and syntax conflicts. To prevent this, React chose className, which matches the exact name of the browser's own DOM property. Writing className avoids collisions with the reserved word while aligning with the native DOM property.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked why JSX differs from HTML, do not just list the syntax rules. Explain that JSX attributes correspond to DOM object properties rather than HTML attribute strings. Mention that className and htmlFor reflect the underlying properties on DOM nodes, and explain that aria-* and data-* are the explicit standard-compliant exceptions to the camelCase rule.

Where you will meet this

  • HTML table row construction: grouping multiple <td> table cells inside <><td>...</td><td>...</td></> without inserting invalid wrapper <div> nodes inside <tr>.
  • Flexbox navigation toolbars: grouping brand logos and navigation links with Fragments so justify-content: space-between distributes items cleanly without intermediate containers.
  • Accessible form input groups: pairing <label htmlFor="subscriber-email"> with <input id="subscriber-email" /> to establish screen reader bindings without layout distortion.
  • Editorial article typography: formatting breaking news stories with self-closing <hr /> dividers and
    line breaks.

Glossary

  • JSX: A syntax extension for JavaScript that allows developers to write declarative HTML-like markup that compiles into JavaScript object descriptors.
  • Fragment: A built-in React component written as <>...</> that groups multiple sibling elements without rendering a physical wrapper node into the DOM tree.
  • Single Root Rule: The syntactic constraint requiring every JSX return statement to have exactly one top-level enclosing element or Fragment.
  • Self-Closing Tag: A JSX element syntax terminating in /> that is mandatory for void elements such as images, inputs, and horizontal rules.
  • Reserved Word: A keyword reserved by the JavaScript language specification that cannot be used as an unquoted property name or variable identifier in standard code.

Summary

JSX Syntax Rules and Fragment Architecture

In daily production, mastering JSX syntax rules ensures that your components compile cleanly and generate optimal DOM structures. While HTML parsers tolerate missing tags and loose attributes, JSX enforces strict language constraints because every tag compiles directly into a JavaScript function call. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ Syntactic Rigor and Fragment Architecture
  1. Return a single root element using React Fragments to prevent layout breakage and DOM bloat.
        (a) Functions in JavaScript cannot return multiple independent objects from a single return statement.
        (b) Fragments group sibling elements without injecting unwanted wrapper nodes into the physical browser DOM.
  2. Enforce explicit closure and camelCase attribute naming across all JSX markup.
        (a) All void elements like images and inputs must terminate with a self-closing forward slash.
        (b) Replace reserved words with DOM property names like className and htmlFor, while keeping aria-* hyphenated.

➔ NEVER leave void elements unclosed or return multiple adjacent JSX tags without a root.

➔ ALWAYS use Fragments (<>...</>) to group sibling elements without adding wrapper divs.

➔ IF writing CSS class names or label targets THEN use className and htmlFor.

DO THIS: Use Fragments to group sibling elements and self-closing tags for void elements.

StoryLead.jsx
1export default function StoryLead() {
2 return (
3 <>
4 <p className="lead-text">City council votes on zoning.</p>
5 <span className="read-time">4 minute read</span>
6 </>
7 );
8}

DO NOT DO THIS: Never return multiple sibling elements without a root or leave void tags unclosed.

StoryLead.jsx
1export default function StoryLead() {
2 return (
3 <p class="lead-text">City council votes on zoning.</p>
4 <span class="read-time">4 minute read</span>
5 );
6}

Lecture 5: JavaScript in JSX: Curly Braces and Dynamic Expressions

Interview Question

CORE

How do you use JavaScript expressions inside JSX with curly braces?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. A developer named Sofia builds a breaking news banner for The National Times website.
  2. Sofia writes the variable reporterCount directly into the JSX text to display staff numbers.
  3. She saves the file and loads the webpage to verify the new banner.
  4. Why does the banner show the literal word "reporterCount" instead of the number?
  5. Static placeholder text misinforms readers and hides critical news updates across the website.
  6. JSX treats text as plain characters unless curly braces open a JavaScript window.
  7. Today you learn how curly braces evaluate dynamic text, attributes, and JavaScript objects.

Opening the JavaScript Portal: The Power of Curly Braces

When you author markup in JSX, any plain text you type between tags is treated as static text. If you type <h2 className="title">headline</h2> the browser renders the exact letters h-e-a-d-l-i-n-e. Even if you declared a JavaScript variable named headline on the line directly above your return statement, JSX has no way of knowing that you intended to reference a variable rather than display literal text.

To bridge the gap between static markup and dynamic memory, React introduces curly braces ({ }). In modern documentation, this mechanism is called JSX Curly Brace Expressions (and referred to classically as JSX Interpolation / Embedded Expressions). In physical browser execution, curly braces tell the compiler to evaluate the enclosed JavaScript variable and pass the resulting value as an argument to the element creation function.

Writing curly braces inside JSX opens an evaluation portal. Outside the braces, you are writing declarative markup structure. Inside the braces, the markup pauses, and you are back in live JavaScript execution. React evaluates the variable or expression, retrieves its active value from memory, and projects the result directly into the rendered DOM node.

⚡ IN THE WILD

What does a curly brace really do? When you write plain text inside JSX tags, the browser treats it as literal text. If you write the word headline, the screen displays the word headline. How do you tell the computer to stop reading text and start running code? You wrap the word in curly braces: {headline}. The curly brace acts as a portal. Inside the braces, you are back in regular JavaScript. You can read variables, add numbers, or run calculations. It is a live portal into JavaScript, time and time again. Wrapping your tokens in curly braces ensures that your JavaScript expressions evaluate dynamically instead of rendering as literal text.

Expressions versus Statements: The Value Requirement

While curly braces allow you to execute JavaScript inside your markup, they do not allow arbitrary JavaScript code. There is an essential syntactic constraint known as the value requirement: you can only place JavaScript expressions inside JSX curly braces; JavaScript statements are strictly forbidden.

To write robust React components, you must understand the difference between an expression and a statement:

  1. A JavaScript expression is any piece of code that evaluates to a single value. Expressions can be passed as arguments to functions, assigned to variables, and evaluated inside curly braces. Valid expressions include variable identifiers ({headline}), property lookups ({author.name}), arithmetic calculations ({elapsedMinutes * 60}), template literals ({${city} Edition}), function invocations ({formatDate(timestamp)}), and ternary conditional operators ({isUrgent ? 'Alert' : 'Update'}).
  2. A JavaScript statement is an imperative language instruction that performs an action or controls program flow, but produces no value. Statements include conditional blocks (if (...) { ... }), loops (for, while), and declarations (let x = 10 function calculate() {}). Because statements do not evaluate to a value, placing an if statement or a for loop inside curly braces triggers an immediate compile-time syntax crash: Unexpected token.

Key Takeaway

Expressions evaluate to a value; statements do not. Only expressions belong in curly braces.

When you need conditional logic inside JSX, you cannot use an if statement. Instead, you use expressions that resolve to values, such as the ternary operator (condition ? valueA : valueB) or the logical AND operator (condition && value).

To see how expressions drive dynamic content on The National Times, examine our breaking news banner. The parent component NewsBanner.jsx renders an urgency notice via AlertNotice.jsx alongside headline details via StoryDetails.jsx:

On the right, the rendered canvas displays the completed banner: an urgent notice reading "Breaking Alert", directly followed by the headline "Severe Storm Warning" and the timestamp "Updated 2 minutes ago". Every string was evaluated dynamically through curly braces.

Let us inspect our first child component, AlertNotice.jsx:

When React evaluates AlertNotice, the condition resolves isUrgent to true, instantly projecting the resulting string 'Breaking Alert' into the DOM span without intermediate variables.

Now examine our second child component, StoryDetails.jsx:

Directly below it, the expression {elapsedMinutes} embeds a numerical value alongside surrounding static text. React automatically converts the number 2 into text and writes the complete sentence into the browser paragraph.

Now examine the parent container, NewsBanner.jsx:
